title: Two_Dimensional Ecological Niche of Pulsatrix perspicillata
text: The spectacled owl (Pulsatrix perspicillata) is a widely distributed Neotropical species associated with a range of environments, including humid and dry tropical forests, wetlands, and savannas. In Costa Rica, it is primarily nocturnal and may use both forest interiors and edges to forage. Analyzing its records in relation to variables such as elevation, mean annual temperature, and human footprint helps describe some of the environmental conditions in which it has been observed. However, these associations alone do not demonstrate habitat preference or explain the causes of its distribution. IUCN Red List, Área de Conservación Guanacaste.

title: Two_Dimensional Ecological Niche of Pulsatrix perspicillata

title: Two_Dimensional Ecological Niche of Pulsatrix perspicillata
text:
Objetive
To describe the distribution of Pulsatrix perspicillata records in Costa Rica and their relationship to elevation, mean annual temperature, and human footprint by comparing them with the background environmental conditions shown in the figures..

title: Two_Dimensional Ecological Niche of Pulsatrix perspicillata
text:
Metodology
Occurrence records of Pulsatrix perspicillata in Costa Rica were analyzed. Coordinates were represented in the WGS84 coordinate reference system. For the temporal analysis, records were classified into two periods: before 2000 and from 2000 onward.
Raster layers of mean annual temperature, annual precipitation, elevation, and human footprint were used. To make them comparable, they were adjusted to the same extent and spatial resolution: the elevation layer was cropped, and the human footprint layer was resampled using bilinear interpolation.
Environmental values were then extracted for each record and compared with values from the available raster cells, which were used as an environmental background. Maps of the records and scatterplots were produced to visualize relationships among environmental variables and compare records between periods. Figures were exported as JPG files at 300 dpi.
The procedure is descriptive and exploratory: the script does not perform statistical tests or model the species’ distribution.

title: Two_Dimensional Ecological Niche of Pulsatrix perspicillata
text:
Kernel density methodology
Records of Pulsatrix perspicillata were cleaned by converting coordinates to numeric format, removing duplicate localities, and retaining those that intersect Costa Rica. The points were then projected to CRTM05 so distances could be calculated in meters.
A Gaussian kernel density surface was estimated using a bandwidth of 5,000 m and 500 m cells. The surface was cropped and masked to the boundaries of Costa Rica, and values were expressed as recorded localities per km².
Polygons representing 50% and 95% of the cumulative density were delineated. The 50% polygon represents areas with the highest concentration of records, while the 95% polygon covers a broader region. These results describe the concentration of recorded localities; they do not represent individual abundance or confirmed distribution boundaries.

title: Two_Dimensional Ecological Niche of Pulsatrix perspicillata
text:
Interpretations
Figure 1. Elevation and records in Costa Rica. The map shows an elevation gradient: green areas correspond to lower elevations, while yellow, orange, and lighter tones indicate higher terrain. The black points appear across different parts of the country, with visible concentrations in the north and central regions. If these points represent records of the species, they suggest that it has been observed across a range of elevations. The map shows elevation and point locations; on its own, it does not identify areas of higher habitat suitability.
Figure 2. Human footprint and elevation. Occurrence records (red) are concentrated mainly at low and intermediate elevations, although some appear at higher elevations. Background points (gray) cover a broader range of conditions. Since these points represent reference areas and are not necessarily locations where the species is absent, the figure allows comparison with available conditions but is not sufficient to conclude that the species prefers specific levels of human footprint. The figure also does not specify the units of the human-footprint axis.
Figure 3. Mean annual temperature and elevation. A clear inverse relationship is visible: locations at higher elevations tend to have lower mean temperatures. Most records (red) cluster at low and intermediate elevations and relatively warm temperatures; a few occur in colder, higher-elevation conditions. Since temperature and elevation vary together in the figure, the pattern cannot be attributed to either variable alone.

title: Two_Dimensional Ecological Niche of Pulsatrix perspicillata
text:
Conclusions

Los registros representados abarcan condiciones ambientales diversas, pero se concentran sobre todo en elevaciones bajas e intermedias.
La distribución de los puntos de ocurrencia sigue el gradiente conjunto de elevación y temperatura; las figuras no permiten separar el efecto de cada variable.
La relación con la huella humana requiere análisis adicional, considerando la escala del índice y el esfuerzo de muestreo.

title: Diversity Indices I y II
text: Biological diversity can be described in terms of species richness and the distribution of species abundances. Rank-abundance curves allow these features to be compared across sites: a longer curve represents greater richness, while its slope provides a visual indication of evenness and the dominance of the most common species. Mapping localities by ecoregion also helps show how records are distributed across different environments. These figures allow comparisons among three sites, although they do not, on their own, explain the causes of the observed patterns.

title: Diversity Indices I y II
text: Biological diversity can be described in terms of species richness and the distribution of species abundances. Rank-abundance curves allow these features to be compared across sites: a longer curve represents greater richness, while its slope provides a visual indication of evenness and the dominance of the most common species. Mapping localities by ecoregion also helps show how records are distributed across different environments. These figures allow comparisons among three sites, although they do not, on their own, explain the causes of the observed patterns.

title: Diversity Indices I y II
text:
Objetive
To compare the spatial distribution of records across ecoregions and describe differences in species richness, dominance, and evenness among Sites 1, 2, and 3 using the rank-abundance curve.

title: Diversity Indices I y II
text:
Metodology
Records from the ccb_dataset were grouped by site and species. Sampling locations were mapped in WGS84 alongside the Coachella Valley boundary, surrounding ecoregion, and Salton Sea.
Species record counts were summarized for each site and sampling plot, and community matrices were created. Alpha diversity was calculated by site and plot using total records (N), species richness (S), Shannon diversity, Simpson diversity, dominance, and Pielou’s evenness. Gamma diversity was calculated for the pooled dataset.
Between-site beta similarity was assessed from presence–absence data using Jaccard and Sørensen indices. Results were visualized with rank-abundance curves, plot-level alpha diversity comparisons, relative abundance of the 15 most frequently recorded species, and a Jaccard similarity heatmap. Figures were exported as JPG files at 300 dpi.

title: Diversity Indices I y II
text:
Results



Figure 1. Spatial distribution of records from Sites 1–3 across four ecoregions. Point colors indicate sites; background colors indicate ecoregions.





Figure 2. Rank-abundance curves for Sites 1–3, showing relative species abundance by rank on a logarithmic scale.

title: Diversity Indices I y II
text:
Interpretations
Figure 1. Records by site and ecoregion. Records from the three sites are distributed unevenly among the ecoregions shown. Site 2 (green) appears widely across the northern and eastern parts of the map, mainly in areas of the Mojave Desert ecoregion. Site 1 (blue) is more concentrated in central and southern areas, while records from Site 3 (pink) are fewer and occur in localized clusters. Records from different sites occur close together in some areas, suggesting some spatial overlap. The red outline marks an area, but the figure does not include a legend explaining what it represents.
Figure 2. Rank-abundance curves. Sites 1 and 2 have longer curves, with approximately 28 and 27 species, respectively, while Site 3 has about 12. Thus, Site 1 has the greatest observed species richness and Site 3 the lowest. Site 2 begins with a higher relative abundance for the top-ranked species, suggesting greater dominance by that species. The curve for Site 1 extends slightly farther into the less abundant species. At Site 3, abundance declines gradually through much of the curve, although there is a marked drop in the final ranks. These differences are descriptive; a formal comparison of evenness or diversity would require abundance data and the corresponding indices.

title: Diversity Indices I y II
text:
Conclusions

Records from the three sites are not distributed evenly across the ecoregions; the map shows clusters and some spatial overlap.
Based on curve length, Sites 1 and 2 have greater observed species richness than Site 3.
Site 2 appears to have greater dominance by its most abundant species, while differences in evenness among sites require quantitative analysis.

title: Spatial Distribution Patterns in Plant Species
text:
Introduction
In population ecology, the study of spatial distribution is important because it helps explain how individuals are arranged within a given area (Borregaard et al., 2008) and is essential for drawing inferences about the processes that shape population dynamics and structure (Hernández-Cruz et al., 2025). In plants in particular, studying spatial distribution has helped identify how some species disperse, their environmental requirements, and even their interactions with other species (Ben-Said, 2021). Based on how individuals are arranged in space, three spatial patterns are recognized: random, uniform, and clumped (Rockwood, 2006). A clumped distribution is characterized by groups of individuals and is usually associated with shared preferences for certain environmental conditions and food resources (Borregaard et al., 2008).
A uniform distribution, on the other hand, is associated with species whose individuals are evenly spaced because of competition for resources, territoriality, or density-dependent mortality related to neighboring individuals (Stoll & Bergius, 2005). Less commonly, species are distributed randomly (Fangliang et al., 1997), a pattern that tends to occur when resources are distributed homogeneously (De Freitas Alves & De Santana, 2022). However, the interpretation of distribution patterns depends on the scale of the study (Levin, 1992).
Ecological processes may shape observed distribution patterns. These include interactions among individuals and dispersal (Vinatier et al., 2011). In practice, quadrat sampling makes it possible to count the individuals within a defined area and estimate their density. Abundance is then compared among sampling units, and statistical measures such as the mean and variance are used to determine the spatial distribution pattern (De Freitas Alves & De Santana, 2022).
This study determined the spatial distribution of Elephantopus mollis (Kunth) and Rhynchospora nervosa (Vahl) Boeckeler. E. mollis (Figure 1A) is a perennial species in the family Asteraceae, with a broad distribution throughout the subtropics and tropics (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, n.d.). It is a strong competitor: it forms dense rosettes that commonly prevent other plant species from growing through competitive exclusion. It also has a germination rate of 80% across a broad temperature range, from 21 to 34°C (Guerra et al., 2026). R. nervosa (Figure 1B), in contrast, is a perennial species in the family Cyperaceae that grows preferentially in seasonally dry climates (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, n.d.). It has a rhizomatous growth form, producing clusters of stems from an underground structure (Gómez-Laurito, 2009). An allelopathic effect on other plants has been documented for this species, as it inhibited the germination and early growth of Vigna unguiculata seedlings (Bezerra et al., 2026).

title: Spatial Distribution Patterns in Plant Species
text:
Objetive
The objectives of this study were to evaluate and compare the spatial distribution patterns of these two plant species using abundance data obtained from quadrats. The null hypothesis was that, for each species, abundance among sampling units would be consistent with a random spatial distribution. The alternative hypothesis was that abundance would not be consistent with a random distribution. Based on preliminary observations, our first prediction was that Elephantopus mollis would show a clumped distribution, whereas our second prediction was that Rhynchospora nervosa would show a pattern consistent with a random distribution.

title: Spatial Distribution Patterns in Plant Species
text:
Metodology

Study area
Sampling took place in an area of herbaceous vegetation and scattered trees within the Recreational Park of the University for Peace, located in the protected area of El Rodeo, Mora, San José, Costa Rica (9° 55′ 9.09″ N, 84° 16′ 21.29″ W), at an elevation of 784 m above sea level. Sampling was conducted on October 6, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The site has rolling topography, scattered mature trees, and visible variation in vegetation cover and soil conditions.


Study species
We studied two herbaceous species with different growth forms. The first, Elephantopus mollis, is an erect herb 0.3–1.5 m tall, with generally hairy stems and alternate, obovate to elliptic leaves with a broadened base and toothed margins (Tropicos.org, 2026; Figure 1A). Plants that could be recognized as independent individuals were counted. The second, Rhynchospora nervosa, is a perennial herb 10–70 cm tall. It grows in clumps or from rhizomes and has narrow leaves (Tropicos.org, 2026; Figure 1B). Each independent clump, or one clearly separated from other clumps, was considered an individual. Individual stems were not counted separately.


Sampling design
A 100 × 100 m study area (1 ha) was delineated and divided into 50 sectors measuring 10 × 20 m. One 1 × 1 m quadrat was randomly established within each sector, for a total of 50 quadrats. A reference point (0,0) was established for the study area to determine the spatial coordinates (X and Y, in meters) of each quadrat within its sector. The sampling units were divided between two groups of four people, and the two data sets were later combined into a single database. For each quadrat, the number of E. mollis and R. nervosa individuals was recorded. Environmental variables were not considered in the sampling and therefore were not included as evidence of the processes responsible for the observed patterns.


Data analysis
Data processing and analysis were conducted in R version 4.6.1 (R Core Team, 2026) using RStudio (Posit team, 2026) and functions from the “Tidyverse” package, version 2.0.0 (Wickham et al., 2019). The dispersion index (DI), defined as the ratio of the sample variance to the sample mean, was calculated to characterize the spatial pattern. DI values below 1 indicate a uniform distribution; values close to 1 suggest a random distribution; and values greater than 1 indicate a clumped distribution.
A chi-square (χ²) test was used to assess whether the observed distribution differed from randomness. Based on the significance level and the distribution indicated by the data, the fit of theoretical probability models was assessed: a binomial distribution for E. mollis and a Poisson distribution for R. nervosa, using functions from the “MASS” package, version 7.3-66 (Venables et al., 2002). The goodness of fit of the data to each distribution was evaluated with a chi-square goodness-of-fit test. The significance level for statistical decisions was set at 5%.
The main results were organized in a table using the “gt” package, version 1.3.0 (Iannone et al., 2020). Point plots were produced to visualize the spatial distribution within the study area, and bar charts and trend lines were used to visualize how well the data fit the distributions, using “ggplot2” (Wickham, 2016). The figures were finalized and assembled with the “cowplot” package, version 1.2.0 (Wilke, 2025).

title: Spatial Distribution Patterns in Plant Species
text:
Results
The dispersion index for Elephantopus mollis was greater than 1 (χ² = 191.8, df = 49, P < 0.001), indicating a clumped distribution that differed from randomness, with variance considerably greater than the mean (Table 1; Figure 2). This behavior is characteristic of counts with high spatial aggregation. The chi-square goodness-of-fit test found no statistically significant difference between the observed data and the expected negative binomial distribution, indicating that the E. mollis counts fit this probability model well (χ² = 0.3, df = 2, P = 0.871; Figure 3A). This result agrees with the clumped spatial pattern identified earlier and with the observed overdispersion.
For Rhynchospora nervosa, there was no evidence that the observed abundance differed from a random spatial pattern (χ² = 48.0, df = 49, P = 0.512; Figure 1B). This agrees with the calculated DI, which was close to 1 and indicates random dispersion in the study area. The goodness-of-fit test also showed an adequate fit to the Poisson distribution (χ² = 2.8, df = 2, P = 0.249; Figure 3B), consistent with the random distribution of this species.

title: Spatial Distribution Patterns in Plant Species
text:
Interpretations
The results showed that Elephantopus mollis had a more clumped distribution because individuals were more concentrated in some quadrats than in others. This agrees with the overdispersion indicated by the DI, which was greater than 1, while the chi-square test showed a statistically significant departure from randomness. The counts also tended to fit a negative binomial distribution, indicating high variation among the study quadrats. The accumulation of individuals and possible preference for certain sites could contribute to this clumping, considering that the species can germinate under a wide range of environmental conditions that may influence this pattern (Guerra et al., 2026).
Regarding R. nervosa, Mora-Fernández and Peñuela-Recio (2013) note that this species has a broad distribution and can adapt to infertile sites such as savannas and pastures. It is also found in dry, humid, rain, and cloud forests. This suggests that its adaptive plasticity allows it to occur in many types of sites without depending on a clumped distribution around a particular resource. The dispersion index obtained (0.98) indicates random dispersion across the quadrats. This is also consistent with an untested hypothesis that homogeneous site conditions may allow a distribution not constrained by specific resources. The mean abundance was 2.30 individuals per quadrat, and the variance was 2.26.
Consistent with these results, the chi-square test supports the decision not to reject the null hypothesis, indicating that the data are close to a random distribution model. The goodness-of-fit test values show an adequate fit to the Poisson distribution, which is compatible with a random spatial pattern.
Spatial distribution alone does not allow us to infer the ecological processes underlying it. However, it is very useful when combined with more focused ecological studies. Other studies identify members of the Cyperaceae family, including the genus Rhynchospora, as pioneer and generalist species with high colonization capacity (Valois-Cuesta & Martínez-Ruiz, 2017). Thus, combining ecological studies with spatial distribution studies can contribute to our understanding of the processes that shape species distributions.
Finally, differences in the spatial distributions of the two species may be related to their traits, such as the rosette growth form of E. mollis and the rhizomatous growth form of R. nervosa. Since both species were found at a site with herbaceous vegetation, scattered trees, rolling terrain, and variation in vegetation cover, their growth forms could be observed under the same general site conditions. E. mollis was found in clusters averaging more than seven individuals, consistent with reports that this species can form dense rosettes that spread and displace other species through competitive exclusion (Guerra et al., 2026). R. nervosa, by contrast, showed a different distribution. Its rhizomatous growth allows it to explore the surrounding area more extensively and spread laterally, which may favor the colonization of available patches (Herben & Klimešová, 2020).

title: Spatial Distribution Patterns in Plant Species
text:
Conclusions
Among the practical limitations of this study, it is important to consider how the scale of observation may have influenced the observed distribution patterns, as well as the composition and structure of the study area. Replicating the study in contrasting ecosystems is therefore recommended to better understand spatial distribution patterns. It is also important to assess the influence of environmental variables such as vegetation cover, temperature, and soil acidity. Finally, the methodology should be standardized through periodic repeated sampling over time to observe how the species behave as part of the natural assemblage within the landscape.

Objective
To describe the spatial concentration of Pulsatrix perspicillata records in Costa Rica using KDE maps and identify areas with higher and lower record density.

A Gaussian kernel density surface was estimated using a 5,000 m bandwidth and 500 m cells. The surface was cropped and masked to Costa Rica, and values were expressed as recorded localities per km².

Results

title: Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of Pulsatrix perspicillata

Interpretations
Figure 1. KDE contours and locality records. The map appears to overlay occurrence points with shaded or outlined density areas. The most concentrated patches are visible in the north-central and central parts of the country, with smaller clusters elsewhere. Because the figure has no visible legend, the density values and color categories cannot be specified.
Figure 2. KDE density surface. The pale-yellow areas represent lower record density, while green, teal, and dark-blue areas represent progressively higher density. The strongest clusters appear in the central and north-central interior; most other areas show lower density, with records dispersed across the country. The legend reports density in localities per square kilometer, reaching approximately 2 localities/km² at the upper end shown.

title: Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of Pulsatrix perspicillata
text:
Conclusions

Both figures show that records are spatially clustered rather than evenly distributed across Costa Rica.
The highest KDE values occur in localized areas, especially in the central and north-central parts of the country.
These maps show the density of records, not owl abundance or habitat suitability; record density may also reflect where observations were collected.

title: Downloading Occurrence Records from GBIF and iNaturalist
text:
Occurrence records show where a species has been observed. They can be used to examine how observations are distributed across different locations and to identify patterns that may help assess whether the species is at risk or whether certain factors influence its distribution.
This study examines the geographic distribution of Pulsatrix perspicillata, commonly known in Costa Rica as the spectacled owl, or “oropopo.” To gather as many records as possible, the study uses reliable sources that document biodiversity observations, including iNaturalist and the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF).
However, occurrence records may contain errors or missing information, which can affect the reliability of a study. It is therefore important to clean the downloaded data and retain accurate, relevant records to support sound interpretation of the results.

This study examines the geographic distribution of Pulsatrix perspicillata, commonly known in Costa Rica as the spectacled owl, or “oropopo.” To gather as many records as possible, the study uses reliable sources that document biodiversity observations, including iNaturalist and the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF).
However, occurrence records may contain errors or missing information, which can affect the reliability of a study. It is therefore important to clean the downloaded data and retain accurate, relevant records to support sound interpretation of the results.

title: Downloading Occurrence Records from GBIF and iNaturalist
text:
Objetive
To download occurrence records for Pulsatrix perspicillata from iNaturalist and GBIF, clean the data by identifying records with missing or questionable information, and use the curated dataset to analyze the species’ geographic distribution across the provinces and cantons of Costa Rica.

title: Downloading Occurrence Records from GBIF and iNaturalist
text:
Metodology
First, RStudio was connected to the GBIF and iNaturalist platforms. Occurrence records were then downloaded from both sources and imported into RStudio to check their content and structure. The records were cleaned and transformed using packages such as tidyverse. Costa Rica’s provincial and cantonal boundary layers were also prepared and converted to the WGS 84 coordinate reference system (EPSG:4326) to ensure consistency with the occurrence coordinates. This process produced a cleaned and organized dataset of Pulsatrix perspicillata records for spatial analysis.
The occurrence coordinates were converted into spatial objects and overlaid with boundary layers, including the canton layer, so that administrative information could be assigned to each observation. Finally, records were counted by province and canton.

title: Downloading Occurrence Records from GBIF and iNaturalist
text:
Results



Figure 1. Number of P. perspicillata Observations in Costa Rica.





Figure 3. A Species Distribution Study Using iNaturalist and GBIF Data: Pulsatrix perspicillata

title: Downloading Occurrence Records from GBIF and iNaturalist
text:
Interpretations
Occurrence records show that Pulsatrix perspicillata has been observed throughout Costa Rica, with clusters of records in several areas. These patterns reflect where observations have been reported, but they may not represent the species’ true abundance because the data are influenced by sampling and observer effort.

title: Downloading Occurrence Records from GBIF and iNaturalist
text:
Conclusions
In conclusion, occurrence records show that Pulsatrix perspicillata has been observed across several parts of Costa Rica, with the highest concentrations of reports in a lot of zones of Costa Rica.

title: Creating and Integrating Quarto Pages into the Scientific Portfolio
text:
Objetive

Create a basic Quarto template for documenting course exercises.
Create new pages from the template without modifying the original file.
Use Visual Mode to edit Quarto documents.
Add text, figures, and tables.
Add references generated with Zotero.
Render a Quarto page.
Integrate a new page into the scientific portfolio.
Publish changes using Git and GitHub Pages.

title: Creating and Integrating Quarto Pages into the Scientific Portfolio
text:
Metodology
Esta práctica se divide en cuatro partes:

Parte I: Crear la plantilla de las prácticas
Paso I: Abrir el proyecto del portafolio.

Abrir el proyecto Scientific-portpolio
Abrir GitHub simultaneamente
Desde el panel files en el proyecto Scientific-portfolio de RStudio comprobar que están los archivos:

_quarto.yml
index.qmd
about.qmd
portfolio.qmd o portafolio.qmd
carpeta images


*Todo esto debe crearse dentro del proyecto asociado a la página Web Scientific-portfolio.
Paso II: Crear nuevo documento Quarto

Ir a File > New File > Quarto Document

En la ventana que aparece:

Seleccione Document.
En Title, escriba:

Título de la práctica

En Author, escriba su nombre.
Seleccione HTML.
Seleccione Visual como editor, si aparece esta opción.
Presione Create.

Paso III: Guardar el archivo como plantilla
Seleccione:
File → Save As
Guarde el archivo con el nombre:
plantilla.qmd
El archivo debe quedar dentro de la carpeta principal del proyecto del sitio web.
* Utilice nombres de archivos sencillos, sin espacios, tildes ni caracteres especiales.
Paso IV: Trabajar en Visual Mode
Compruebe que se encuentra trabajando en Visual Mode.
Si fuera necesario, seleccione Visual en la parte superior del editor.
Visual Mode permite editar el documento de manera similar a Microsoft Word.
Paso V: Construir la Estructura de la Plantilla
Debajo del título del documento agregue las siguientes secciones utilizando Heading 2.
Aquí se introducen los apartados del documento, tales como:

Introduction

Breve descripción del tema de la práctica y su importancia.

Objetive

Indique el objetivo principal de la práctica.

Metodology

Describa brevemente las actividades realizadas y los métodos utilizados.
No es necesario incluir todos los códigos de R utilizados durante el laboratorio.

Resultados

Presente los principales resultados obtenidos durante la práctica.
Esta sección puede incluir:

texto;
figuras;
fotografías;
gráficos;
mapas;
cuadros.


Interpretations

Explique qué significan los resultados obtenidos.
Considere preguntas como:

¿Cuál fue el patrón más importante?
¿Qué indican las figuras o cuadros?
¿Cómo se relacionan los resultados con el objetivo de la práctica?


Conclusions

Resuma brevemente las principales conclusiones o aprendizajes de la práctica.

Bibliography

Resuma brevemente las principales conclusiones o aprendizajes de la práctica.


Paso VI: Guardar Plantilla
Guarde los cambios:
Ctrl + S
Al finalizar debe existir el archivo:
plantilla.qmd
Importante: plantilla.qmd será nuestro archivo original. De ahora en adelante no escribiremos directamente sobre esta plantilla. Para cada nueva práctica crearemos una copia.


Parte II: Crear una práctica a partir de la Plantilla
Ahora utilizaremos plantilla.qmd para crear la página correspondiente a la práctica de Zotero realizada la semana anterior.

Abra plantilla.qmd.
Seleccione File → Save As.
Guarde la copia con el nombre:
zotero.qmd
Compruebe que está trabajando en Visual Mode.
Cambie el título por:
Gestión de referencias bibliográficas con Zotero
Complete brevemente las secciones de la plantilla utilizando el trabajo realizado durante la práctica anterior.
Importante: no modifique plantilla.qmd. Esta se conservará para crear las próximas prácticas.

Insertar figuras
Se incorpora una figura sencilla para prácticar la inserción de imágenes en Quarto.

Abra Zotero y seleccione la colección creada durante la práctica anterior.
Tome una captura de pantalla donde se observe la colección y algunas de las referencias incorporadas.
Guarde la imagen dentro de la carpeta images del proyecto del sitio web con el nombre:
zotero_biblioteca.png
Regrese a zotero.qmd y coloque el cursor en la sección Resultados.
En Visual Mode, seleccione Insert → Figure.
Seleccione zotero_biblioteca.png.
Agregue como pie de figura:
Ejemplo de una colección de referencias bibliográficas organizada en Zotero.

Compruebe que la figura aparece correctamente en el documento.

title: Creating and Integrating Quarto Pages into the Scientific Portfolio
text:
Insertar cuadros
En la sección Resultados, debajo de la figura, inserte un cuadro para resumir las formas de incorporar referencias utilizadas durante la práctica.

En Visual Mode, seleccione Insert → Table.
Cree un cuadro de 2 columnas y 5 filas.
Complete el cuadro de la siguiente manera:








Método
¿Cuándo utilizarlo?




DOI
Cuando la publicación tiene un DOI conocido


Archivo RIS
Cuando la revista o base de datos permite exportar la referencia


Zotero Connector
Para capturar referencias directamente desde el navegador


Entrada manual
Cuando la información no puede importarse automáticamente




Agregue como título:
Métodos utilizados para incorporar referencias bibliográficas a Zotero.


Parte III: Incorporar las referencias de Zotero.
Ahora utilizaremos las referencias trabajadas durante la práctica anterior para insertar citas en zotero.qmd.
Exportar referencias

Abra Zotero.
Seleccione la colección utilizada durante la práctica.
Haga clic derecho sobre la colección y seleccione Export Collection.
Seleccione el formato BibTeX.
Guarde el archivo dentro del proyecto del sitio web con el nombre:
referencias.bib
Regrese a RStudio y compruebe en el panel Files que aparece el archivo:
referencias.bib
*No continuar hasta comprobar que referencias.bib aparece en el panel Files.

Conectar Referencias con Zotero.qmd
Una vez que referencias.bib existe dentro del proyecto:

Abra zotero.qmd.
Cambie momentáneamente de Visual a Source.
Localice el encabezado YAML que aparece al inicio del documento.
Agregue la siguiente línea antes de format:

bibliography: referencias.bib
Ejemplo:

Guarde el archivo.
Regrese a Visual Mode.
*Esta modificación se realiza en zotero.qmd, no en plantilla.qmd.

Insertar Citas

Coloque el cursor en el texto donde desea insertar una referencia.
En Visual Mode, seleccione Insert → Citation.
Busque la referencia correspondiente.
Selecciónela e inserte la cita.

Inserte al menos una referencia utilizada durante la práctica.
Presione Render y compruebe que la cita y la bibliografía aparecen correctamente.


Parte IV: Integrar la Práctica al Portafolio
Ahora conectaremos zotero.qmd con el cajón que ya existe en el sitio web.

Abra portafolio.qmd.
Localice el cajón:
Gestión de referencias bibliográficas con Zotero
Elimine el texto Disponible próximamente.
Agregue una descripción breve de la práctica.
Escriba:
Ver práctica →
Seleccione Ver práctica → y utilice la herramienta para insertar un enlace.
Enlace el texto con:
zotero.qmd
Elimine el cajón Próximas prácticas, ya que a partir de ahora las prácticas reales se irán incorporando al portafolio.



Parte V: Actualizar y Publicar el sitio

Guarde todos los cambios.
Seleccione Render Website.
Compruebe que el cajón de Zotero aparece correctamente.
Compruebe que Ver práctica → abre zotero.qmd.

Si todo funciona:

Abra la pestaña Git de RStudio.
Marque los archivos nuevos o modificados.
Seleccione Commit.
Utilice un mensaje como:
Agregar práctica de Zotero
Presione Commit.
Presione Push.
Abra el sitio web publicado y compruebe que la práctica funciona correctamente.



Para las próximas prácticas
De ahora en adelante utilizaremos siempre el mismo procedimiento:
plantilla.qmd → Save As → completar práctica → Render → agregar al portafolio → Render Website → Commit → Push
El proyecto de R del curso se utilizará para trabajar con datos, códigos y análisis. El portafolio científico se utilizará para presentar y comunicar los métodos, resultados, figuras, cuadros, interpretaciones y conclusiones más importantes.

title: Data Organization with Tidyverse
text: La organización y depuración de datos son pasos muy importantes para obtener resultados confiables y puntuales en un análisis estadístico. Para esta se trabajó con dos set de datos, uno uno de registros metereológicos de cinco estaciones y otro de observaciones de ungulados en Angola. Para poder análizar estos datos se utilizó RStudio y también se requirió funciones del paquete tidyverse puesto que requería de algunas correcciones como ordenar variables, corregir su estructura para facilitar su interpretación.

title: Data Organization with Tidyverse
text: La organización y depuración de datos son pasos muy importantes para obtener resultados confiables y puntuales en un análisis estadístico. Para esta se trabajó con dos set de datos, uno uno de registros metereológicos de cinco estaciones y otro de observaciones de ungulados en Angola. Para poder análizar estos datos se utilizó RStudio y también se requirió funciones del paquete tidyverse puesto que requería de algunas correcciones como ordenar variables, corregir su estructura para facilitar su interpretación.

title: Data Organization with Tidyverse
text:
Objetive
The objective of this exercise was to apply data transformations, separation, combination, selection, and grouping to better organize the datasets for later analysis. Tables and graphs were then used to make the results easier to understand.

title: Data Organization with Tidyverse
text:
Metodology
The exercise was conducted in RStudio using functions from packages such as tidyverse. We imported the meteorological and angola_ungulates CSV files from the data folder in the Eco_pc_2026 project and then applied the necessary transformations.

Meteorological data
In the meteorological dataset, the March data were distributed across several columns. We reorganized the data so that each daily observation occupied one row. We then combined the year (2010–2020) and day to create a date, separated maximum and minimum temperatures, and converted several variables to numeric values. After cleaning and transforming the data, we calculated average temperature, precipitation, and snowfall for each station.


Ungulate data
In the ungulate dataset, we created a date from the year, month, and day columns. We also combined the genus and species columns into a single scientific-name column and separated the taxonomic information into class, order, and family. Finally, we counted the number of observations for each species, created a taxonomic table, and plotted the number of observations by species.

title: Data Organization with Tidyverse
text:
Results



Figure 2. Tempertatura promedio según estaciones.





Figure 2. Number of observations by ungulate species in Angola.

title: Data Organization with Tidyverse
text:
Interpretations
The average-temperature plot shows the range between the average minimum temperature, represented by a white circle, and the average maximum temperature, represented by a black circle, over the study period. Berkeley and Chapel Hill 2 W have warmer temperature ranges, whereas Ithaca Cornell Univ and UW Arboretum–Madison have cooler ranges, with average minimum temperatures reaching below 0°C. New York CNTRL PK TWR has an intermediate range. Across all five stations, the average maximum temperature is considerably higher than the average minimum temperature.
The bar chart shows the number of observations for each species included in the analysis. Hippopotamus amphibius has the most observations, followed by Kobus leche. By contrast, Bos taurus has far fewer records. These results show that the number of observations is unevenly distributed among the species.

title: Data Organization with Tidyverse
text:
Conclusions
This exercise provided an opportunity to learn data-cleaning and organization techniques in RStudio using packages such as tidyverse. Although the two datasets were very different, they allowed us to apply several transformations and reorganizations. In the meteorological dataset, separating the temperature measurements made it easier to compare average temperatures across stations. In the ungulate dataset, organizing the taxonomic information made it possible to classify the species and count their observation records.
